items.question: What kinds of fruit and opposing conditions determine a practitioner's qualification?
premises: The fruit may be clear and primary, or it may be a final fruit.
The fruit may belong to the principal element or to its auxiliary.
The fruit may arise in its opposite, in another side, or in another opposing condition.
items.inference: Qualification depends on the specific kind of fruit and the context in which that fruit appears.
uncertainties: The exact syntactic completion of the verse is carried into the following verse.
items.plain_english: The fruit may be clear and primary, or it may be the final result; it may belong to the main element or to an auxiliary; and it may appear in its opposite, in another side, or in some other opposing condition.

items.question: How do bodily suitability and prior preparation affect eligibility for practice?
premises: A person may become a receptacle for manifesting aspects of various opposing conditions.
Such eligibility depends on a suitably prepared body and related factors.
It also depends on one who shares in the appropriate preparatory conditioning.
items.inference: Eligibility is shaped by both the practitioner's embodied condition and their received preparation.
uncertainties: The referent of saṃskārabhāginaḥ could be the teacher, the student, or both in context.
items.plain_english: Even one who becomes a vessel for manifesting aspects of various opposites is affected by having a suitable body and by sharing in the proper preparatory conditioning.

rows.grounds: compound: adhikriyā+kramaḥ; initial a elided after sandhi

items.question: How is the sequence of qualification determined for teacher and student?
premises: A corresponding sequence of qualification is declared for both teacher and student.
This sequence is illustrated by one who undertakes the death-destroying elixir procedure.
The analogy implies that prior preparation governs later ritual eligibility.
items.inference: The order of qualification for teacher and student follows the same logic of preparatory fitness as other regulated procedures.
items.plain_english: Such a sequence of qualification is declared for both teacher and student, just as in the case of someone who undertakes the procedure of the death-destroying elixir.

items.question: Why must preparatory purification precede initiation and later ritual action?
premises: Preparatory conditioning is first obtained through purifying measures such as decoction, vomiting, and purging.
Initiation produces an alteration in the candidate.
That alteration should not occur later during the main ritual procedure.
items.inference: Purification must come before initiation so that disruptive change does not interfere with subsequent ritual performance.
items.plain_english: First, for the sake of gaining the proper preparation, one uses decoction, emesis, and purgation; and the alteration brought about by initiation should not occur later during the ritual procedure.

items.question: Why are Vaishnavas and others restricted from certain Shaiva rites?
premises: Restriction of qualification arises from factors such as the practitioner's body and level of knowledge.
Vaishnavas and others are said to rely on the discipline suited to bound souls.
That discipline does not confer the preparation required for higher Shaiva rites.
items.inference: Because their conditioning belongs to the paśu level, Vaishnavas and others are not qualified for those rites.
uncertainties: The middle compound taddehavidaśādijaḥ is compressed and its exact member boundaries are interpretive.
items.plain_english: Therefore the restriction of qualification arises from factors such as one's body and knowledge; for this reason Vaishnavas and others, who depend on the discipline of bound souls, are spoken of as limited in that way.

items.question: How does qualification differ across the graded Shaiva scriptural domains?
premises: Those outside the Shaiva preparation are not qualified in the Shaiva scripture.
Shaivas qualified at one level are not thereby qualified in the left sphere.
Those of the left and right spheres are not thereby qualified in the Kula doctrine or the Trika.
items.inference: Qualification is graded and does not automatically transfer upward across scriptural domains.
items.plain_english: They are not qualified in the Shaiva scripture; Shaivas are not qualified in the left sphere; those are not qualified in the right; and those are not qualified in the Kula doctrine or in the Trika.

items.question: What kind of teacher is fit to perform the highest initiatory rites?
premises: The revered Bhairava Kula states a standard for the teacher.
A fit teacher is one suited to the rite of the five initiations.
Such a teacher has either transcended the lower streams or is grounded in the Trika scripture.
items.inference: Only a teacher established beyond the lower streams or in the Trika is qualified for the highest initiatory rites.
items.plain_english: It is said in the revered Bhairava Kula that the teacher fit for the rite of the five initiations is one who has transcended the lower streams or who is grounded in the Trika scripture.

items.question: How can qualification be both one and differentiated at the same time?
premises: At the level of reliance on the self-principle, qualification can be described as one.
Preparatory conditioning differs among practitioners.
Difference in preparation produces difference in qualification.
items.inference: Qualification is unitary in its basic locus but differentiated according to preparation.
uncertainties: saṃskārāśraya appears without an explicit case ending in the tokenized form; its relation is inferred from the compound context.
items.plain_english: Thus there is a single qualification insofar as all rely on the self-principle, yet qualification becomes differentiated because of differences in preparation.

items.question: Why can Shiva be said to be the fruit of every scripture?
premises: The Svacchanda Tantra states that Shiva is the fruit in every scripture.
All scriptures arise from Shiva.
What arises from Shiva has Shiva's abode as its fruit.
items.inference: Because all scriptures originate in Shiva, their ultimate fruit is Shiva.
items.plain_english: Therefore it is said in the Svacchanda Tantra that in every scripture Shiva is the fruit, because all arise from Shiva and all have Shiva's abode as their fruit.

items.question: What higher knowledge is said to be inaccessible to Samkhya, Yoga, and Pancharatra?
premises: The same scripture again speaks in the section on discriminating higher principles.
It refers to something not known by the Samkhyas.
It refers to something not known by the great yogins or by the Pancharatrikas.
items.inference: There is a higher principle whose full discrimination lies beyond those systems.
uncertainties: The verse introduces a quotation whose completion continues in the next verse.
items.plain_english: And there again it is declared, in the discussion of the higher principles: what is not known by the Samkhyas, not by the great yogins, and not, O beloved, by the Pancharatrikas.

items.question: Why are the many rival schools said to fall short of knowing Shiva-tattva?
premises: The scripture challenges as many as three hundred and sixty-three disputants.
Those disputants discriminate only within a limited range.
Limited discrimination cannot grasp the full higher principle.
items.inference: The rival schools are rejected because their knowledge extends only to a partial domain.
uncertainties: The number three hundred and sixty-three is taken as a traditional count of rival views.
items.plain_english: Thus, as many as three hundred and sixty-three disputants are challenged, for they discriminate only within that limited measure.

items.question: Can partial knowledge of a fragment amount to knowledge of unlimited Shiva-tattva?
premises: The rival schools know only a limited portion.
Unlimited Shiva-tattva cannot be constituted by a merely partial grasp.
An objection proposes that they might still posit Shiva's presence in that partial portion.
items.inference: A partial grasp does not by itself make them knowers of the unlimited Shiva principle.
items.plain_english: How could they be knowers whose very nature is knowledge of the unlimited Shiva principle? Now suppose they posit the presence of Shiva even in that mere partial portion.

items.question: Why is superimposing the whole of Shiva on a partial view not coherent?
premises: One might try to superimpose Shiva's presence on a mere part.
Such superimposition lacks clear coherence.
A sentence like 'Devadatta' refers to a complete individual, not to a fragment.
items.inference: Superimposing the whole on a part fails because meaning and reference require a coherent whole.
items.plain_english: If they were to superimpose that, it would not be clearly coherent; for in a sentence like 'Devadatta,' the reference is to a complete form in every respect.

items.question: How could a hearer of a partial word recover the meaning of whole prior sentences?
premises: A hearer may grasp only a single limited word such as 'Devadatta'.
The full meaning belongs to entire previous sentences.
A partial word does not by itself contain that whole sentential meaning.
items.inference: One cannot legitimately superimpose the meaning of whole sentences onto a merely partial word.
items.plain_english: How could someone who hears only the word 'Devadatta' superimpose upon that limited word the meaning of entire previous sentences?

items.question: Can full meaning be understood from a sentence if one is only hearing a partial word?
premises: Understanding of the full meaning would have to come from the sentence as a whole.
If one claims it comes merely from that partial word, the hearer is no longer just a word-hearer.
The limited part would then no longer remain merely limited.
items.inference: Full sentential understanding cannot be reduced to hearing a mere fragment without contradiction.
uncertainties: The sentence continues into the next verse for its full conclusion.
items.plain_english: And how could he understand so much meaning from the sentence? If one says, 'just from that,' then he is not merely a hearer of a word, nor—

items.question: What kind of knowledge is required to understand the present Shaiva domain correctly?
premises: A merely partial element does not contain the full meaning.
The present domain concerns the meaning of the Shaiva scripture.
Correct understanding requires knowledge of that meaning in its complete form.
items.inference: In this domain, only complete knowledge of the Shaiva scriptural meaning is adequate.
items.plain_english: —is that the meaning of only that much. Thus, in the present domain, understanding must come through knowledge of the entire meaning of the Shaiva scripture in its complete form.

items.question: Can other scriptural systems be construed as complete through the Shiva principle?
premises: One might try to interpret Yoga, Samkhya, Arhata, Nyaya, Pancharatra, Veda, and Smriti through the Shiva principle.
Such an interpretation would treat them as complete in that light.
The proposal raises the question of whether that completeness is actually present in them.
items.inference: The possibility of reinterpreting other systems through Shiva-tattva is entertained as an objection.
items.plain_english: If one were to construe Yoga, Samkhya, Arhata, Nyaya, Pancharatra, Veda, and Smriti as complete through the Shiva principle—

items.question: Why is reinterpretation through Shiva-tattva insufficient without proper preparation?
premises: One may grant a limited reinterpretation of other systems through Shiva-tattva.
That does not mean the full expansion of Shiva-tattva is present there.
Knowledge of Shiva-tattva must be preceded by the appropriate preparation.
items.inference: Without the requisite preparation, other systems cannot yield full knowledge of Shiva-tattva.
items.plain_english: Let that be granted to that extent; but the full expansion is not there. It has been examined that knowledge of the Shiva principle must be preceded by the proper preparation.

items.question: What happens if teacher and student lack the required preparation for Shiva-tattva?
premises: Knowledge of Shiva-tattva requires the proper preparation.
If that preparation is absent, both teacher and student incur a fault.
If that preparation is received, the scriptural meaning may indeed be understood in that way.
items.inference: The legitimacy of transmitting Shiva-tattva depends on the presence of the required preparation.
items.plain_english: Otherwise there would be a transgression for both teacher and student; but if the proper preparation is received, then the meaning of the scripture may indeed be of that kind.

items.question: Does receiving higher preparation erase a practitioner's former sectarian identity?
premises: A person may receive higher and higher preparation.
Even so, he may continue to practice as a Vaishnava, Samkhya, or follower of Vedic tradition.
Former identity and new preparation do not automatically coincide.
items.inference: Higher preparation alone does not abolish a practitioner's continued adherence to a prior discipline.
items.plain_english: But even after receiving higher and higher preparation, he does not cease to be Vaishnava, Samkhya, or Vedic in identity; he still continues to practice accordingly.

rows.grounds: in that; initial a elided after sandhi

items.question: How can strict sectarian restriction be justified within a nondual standpoint?
premises: If one remains Vaishnava and so on while claiming higher preparation, a serious transgression follows.
An objector asks how such a primary restriction can stand in the nondual state.
The objection challenges whether nonduality permits rigid sectarian boundaries.
items.inference: The text raises a tension between graded qualification and the claim of nonduality.
items.plain_english: Then, if he remains Vaishnava and so on, his transgression is even greater. But surely, in this nondual state, what is this primary conceptual restriction?

items.question: Who is actually committed to duality in this dispute about nonduality?
premises: The objector appeals to nonduality while insisting on sectarian identity.
That insistence is itself shaped by duality.
By clinging to that position, the objector resorts to duality.
items.inference: The objection fails because the objector's own stance is grounded in duality.
items.plain_english: What are you saying? You yourself, whose conduct is struck by duality, have resorted to this very supreme duality.

items.question: Why does claiming Vaishnava identity undermine the objection to Shaiva qualification rules?
premises: The objector says, 'Being a Vaishnava, why am I not qualified in the Shaiva domain?'
This claim presupposes a fixed dualistic identity.
Within duality, restriction operates by force of rule.
items.inference: The objector cannot appeal to nonduality while simultaneously insisting on a dualistic sectarian identity.
items.plain_english: When you say, 'Being a Vaishnava, why am I not qualified in the Shaiva domain?' you yourself are deluded by duality; and in duality, restriction applies by force.

items.question: What follows from sectarian restriction, and how is a deity properly worshiped?
premises: Given the established rules of qualification, transgression would arise from violating them.
This consequence has already been demonstrated.
A deity is worshiped through identification with that deity.
items.inference: Because worship depends on identification, sectarian restriction and its consequences remain operative where dualistic identity persists.
uncertainties: The final tataḥ points forward to the next verse, so the argument continues beyond this unit.
items.plain_english: Therefore, by those rules, transgression would arise; this has been established. Moreover, a deity is worshiped through identification, and so—
